newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan current account surplus drops by almost 20%.
newsitem.headline: Japan current account surplus drops by almost 20%.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, dropped by almost 20 percent in October from a year earlier, the Finance Ministry announced on Wednesday.
The drop of 19.6 percent to 367.4 billion yen ($3.25 billion) was slightly steeper than earlier predictions by economists, but still in line with the recent trend.

"The data were in line with our forecasts. The year-on-year decline in the current account surplus is gradually narrowing. We confirmed that trend," Mamoru Yamazaki of Paribas Capital Markets, Tokyo, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
The current account surplus has been falling on a year-on-year basis every month since December 1994. It totalled 457.1 billion yen ($4.04 billion) in October 1995.
The year-on-year drop in September was 35.6 percent. Economists had expected the pace of the decline to slow in October, due mainly to a slight fall in the trade surplus that month.
The overall trade surplus fell 12.9 percent in October from a year earlier to 470.86 billion yen ($4.16 billion), the 23rd consecutive month it has declined on a year-on-year basis.
Exports have been increasing, led by vehicle shipments to the United States, but import growth is still bigger than that of exports, economists said.

Yamazaki said he expects the year-on-year surplus to continue to shrink for a while, but added that Japan may at some point next year see year-on-year growth in both its current account and trade balance surpluses.
With machinery orders and private capital spending picking up, current economic activity was stronger than generally expected, Yamazaki said.
"But at the same time, everybody is concerned about the weak economic activity due to the planned consumption tax hike next April," Yamazaki said.
Other economists agreed, saying the planned tax increase from three to five percent from April 1, may cut into imports.

"Starting from sometime next year, Japan's surplus may start rising again due to the recent recovery in exports and the slowdown in import volume," Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Tokyo, told RFTV.

Kato said international investors were keeping a close eye on Japan's trade figures and "if the surplus starts growing again, the dollar/yen (rate) may start start moving to trade around 110 or 105 yen sometime next year."
However, a Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said the current account surplus was likely to continue to decline, despite the weakening of the yen against the dollar.

"We conducted hearings and most companies have told us that they basically do not intend to change their overseas production and investment plans despite the weaker yen. I don't think the declining trend will change," the official said.

He said the pace of the decline would slow due to increased exports, but these would not be enough to stop the fall in the surplus as growth in imports continued to exceed that of exports, and there was also a deficit in services trade.
